title: The Talk in Ayodhya
word: each as a lens for a week
hook: Rama hears what the city is saying about Sita: Nyaya asks whose word it is, Vaisheshika asks what you're looking at
carry: nyaya: knowing needs a reliable word, not a rumor
tomorrow: a mother asks her son how to be free.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna's new eyes: darshana, to see and be seen; six ways of seeing. Today, the first pair, through one of the hardest chapters in the Ramayana.

Rama is home. The war is won, Sita is back, and Ayodhya has its king. In the last book of Valmiki's Ramayana, Rama asks a courtier named Bhadra what people in the city are saying. Bhadra hesitates, then tells him. They praise the war. But they talk about Sita: she lived in Ravana's palace, and the king took her back. Later tellings put the words in the mouth of a washerman scolding his own wife. Either way, it's talk. And the king acts on it. Sita, carrying his children, is taken to the forest and left there. Hindus have argued about this chapter for centuries. Today's first pair of lenses shows one way to see why it hurts.
screen: `WHAT IS THE CITY SAYING?` → `TALK ABOUT SITA.` → `THE KING ACTS ON IT.`

segments.voice: First, the Nyaya lens. Its question: how do I know? The Nyaya Sutra names the means of right knowing: perception, inference, comparison, and word. And word counts only when it comes from a reliable person, someone who knows the matter and tells it straight. Click that lens onto Ayodhya. What did the city see? Nothing; they weren't in Lanka. What's left is talk, passed hand to hand by people who don't know. Under Nyaya, that isn't knowledge. It isn't even false yet. It's simply not known. And there was reliable word on the other side: Sita's own, and the fire she walked into in Lanka, which, the Ramayana says, gave her back unharmed. Now the Vaisheshika lens. Its question: what is this made of? Kanada's school sorts the world into categories: substance, quality, action, and more. Many teachers use it this way: a thing isn't the same as one act done around it. The city's talk is the city's act, not a quality of Sita. That's the teaching under today: in Hindu thought, knowing is something you check, not something you catch. Pramana, the means of knowing, has to hold. The playwright Bhavabhuti built a whole play around Rama's grief over this choice; others read it as a king bound to his people's trust. Either way, the two lenses won't let talk pass for knowledge just because it's loud.
screen: `NYAYA: HOW DO I KNOW?` · `WHOSE WORD IS IT?` · `VAISHESHIKA: WHAT IS THIS MADE OF?` · `TALK IS NOT KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you heard lately about a person you know, and ask the Nyaya question: did I see this, reason to it, or hear it, and if I heard it, does the one who said it really know? Then the Vaisheshika question: is this the person, one act of theirs, or only talk about them? Let what isn't known yet stay not known. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer; if you don't, simply wish them well.
Each as a lens for a week. Today, the first pair: Nyaya asks how do I know, Vaisheshika asks what is this made of. Today's word.

howItsDone: Nyaya and Vaisheshika are traditionally studied together, and students of Indian logic learn the Nyaya Sutra's means of knowing, including the rule that word counts only from a reliable person, alongside Vaisheshika's categories of what there is.
